guide.title: Setup guide
guide.subtitle: Tags, reader and kiosk: from the purchase to the first pass at the door.

buy.title: What to buy

tags.em125: 125 kHz tags: EM4100 key fobs or cards, sold as "RFID 125 kHz". Sturdy, no battery, contactless — a fob gets lost less often than a card.
tags.nfc: NFC cards 13.56 MHz: MIFARE Classic, NTAG or any "ISO 14443" card. The bank-card format can be printed on and slipped into a badge holder.
tags.chooseOne: Pick one frequency and keep it: a 125 kHz reader does not read an NFC card, and the other way round.

buy.reader: A USB "keyboard emulation" reader at the same frequency as the tags. It plugs in like a keyboard, needs no software, and types the card number followed by Enter. One reader per kiosk device.

plug.title: Plug in the reader
plug.p1: Plug the reader into the kiosk device: straight into a computer, through an OTG adapter on an Android tablet, through a USB adapter on an iPad. No driver to install: the device sees it as a keyboard. To check, open any text field and pass a tag: its number appears, followed by a line break.
plug.p2: If the reader offers several output formats (10 digits, 8 hexadecimal characters…), pick one and never change it: a tag enrolled in one format is not recognised in the other.

test.title: Test the reader
test.p1: In Settings › Badges and cards, click into the "Reader" field and pass a tag. The line says what was read, how many characters, and whose card it is, without recording a pass. Enter the number length under "Reader and tags": the test then flags every read that does not match.

assign.title: Assign the tags
assign.p1: Click "Assign by scan", select a person in the register and pass their tag: the card is theirs, the selection clears and you move on to the next. From a child's or a team member's record, "Scan a card" does the same for one person.

kiosk.title: At the kiosk
kiosk.p1: Open the kiosk on the device the reader is plugged into. A parent passes their tag: their children's arrival or departure is recorded at the time of the pass. A child's or a team member's tag works the same way. Without a reader, the code printed on the card still works on the keypad or the camera.

lost.title: Lost tag
lost.p1: In the register, open the person's "…" menu and revoke the lost card: it opens nothing any more, as of now. Assign a new one by scan; the history of passes is kept.

office.title: At the desk, while the computer does something else
office.p1: A "keyboard emulation" reader is a keyboard: what it reads goes to the active window. If you are working in a spreadsheet, the pass is typed into the spreadsheet, and no web page can bring itself to the front for a keystroke it never received. Two settings, together, settle it: read the reader through a port instead of the keyboard, and keep a small kiosk window on top of the others.

moves.serial: Switch the reader to "serial port" (USB-COM) mode with the configuration barcode from the manufacturer's sheet: "USB CDC" for Zebra and Symbol, "USB Serial" for Honeywell, "USB virtual COM" for Netum and Inateck. From then on it types nothing into text fields: that is expected.
moves.connect: Open the kiosk in Chrome or Edge on the computer, choose "Serial port", click "Connect the reader" and pick the port from the list. The browser remembers the choice: on the next starts, the kiosk reconnects by itself.
moves.pip: Click "Keep on screen": a small window detaches and stays on top of the others, in a corner of the screen. It is the one that shows "Ready", then the check and the card of every pass, while the rest of the screen serves the spreadsheet or the mail.

office.fallback: If the browser does not offer "Keep on screen" (Firefox, Safari), turn on "Alerts": every pass shows a system notification with the child's name, the direction and the time; the kiosk sound stays, and the tab title blinks in the taskbar.
office.limit: A reader that can only pose as a keyboard cannot do this: what it reads will always go to the active window. Two ways out: a reader that offers a serial mode — most 2D barcode readers, between 3,000 and 6,000 DA — or the tablet that stays at the door.
